title: How To Talk To Difficult Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that most teachers talk to difficult students far too much, mistakenly believing that extra attention itself improves behavior. He offers seven guidelines for making conversations with difficult students actually effective: keeping them infrequent, being honest rather than manipulative, keeping them meaningful (not interrogative), framing them as encouraging challenges, sometimes saying nothing at all, using wordless gestures like a fist bump, and ensuring interactions are free of strings or hidden agendas. He closes by urging teachers to let difficult students face the natural consequences of their mistakes and the genuine joy of their successes, rather than over-narrating the lesson for them.
points: Excessive talking to difficult students — pep-talks, reminders, and lectures — is identified as largely a waste of time and often counterproductive.
Conversations should be infrequent, honest, and meaningful, avoiding interrogative questions like asking why a student misbehaved.
Sometimes the most powerful response to good behavior from a difficult student is saying nothing at all, avoiding the appearance of a 'parade' for expected behavior.
Wordless gestures such as a fist bump or knowing smile are recommended over verbal praise for reinforcing sustained improvement.
Teachers should decide to genuinely like and enjoy difficult students, since 'no strings attached' rapport is what gives later conversations real weight.
quotes: Most teachers talk to difficult students too much, because somewhere along the line they’ve gotten the idea that the more attention they give them, the better teacher they’ll be.
In a desperate attempt to improve behavior, many teachers will say just about anything to difficult students—regardless of its truthfulness.

Never ask them why they did this or that. Never force assurances or explanations. Never give them a dressing-down. Let their mistakes and subsequent accountability, or their successes and subsequent good feelings, be the lesson.
By simply not making a big deal out of them doing what they’re supposed to do, what they’re expected to do, you send a powerful, behavior-altering message.
But the more attention you give to difficult students, the less attention they’ll pay to what you say and the harder it will be to improve their behavior.
